links.outcome: Physician acceptance of AI-drafted replies after iterative, versioned prompt engineering
links.effect: Acceptance of draft suitability rose from 62% to 84% (P<.001) in the validation set (N=200); 74% of production drafts were rated helpful.
links.quote: After 3 iterations of prompt engineering, physician acceptance of draft suitability increased from 62% to 84% (P <.001) in the validation dataset (N = 200), and 74% of drafts in the test dataset were rated as "helpful."

links.outcome: Patient preference for tone and quality after feedback-driven prompt revision
links.effect: Patient preference for optimized prompt (V3) drafts was 62% for tone and quality, versus <15% for the initial prompt (P<.001).
links.quote: When comparing responses created from the final prompt to the initial prompt, patient preference shifted to the optimized prompt (V3) based LLM-generated responses for tone ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%) and quality ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%), significantly higher than preference to the first iteration of prompt based LLM-generated response (<15% for both tone or overall quality) with P -value less than .001.

links.outcome: Hallucinated clinical information in AI-drafted patient message replies
links.effect: 7 (6%) of 116 training-set drafts contained hallucinated information; none in the validation set; 16% of validation drafts rejected by physicians.
links.quote: Interesting, 7 (6%) of the 116 original messages from the test set were found to contain hallucinated information in the LLM responses.

links.outcome: Patient preference for tone and quality after iterative, clinician- and patient-reviewed prompt refinement
links.effect: Patient advisors preferred optimized-prompt responses for tone and quality (N = 154, 62% each), versus <15% for initial-prompt responses (P -value less than .001).
links.quote: When comparing responses created from the final prompt to the initial prompt, patient preference shifted to the optimized prompt (V3) based LLM-generated responses for tone ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%) and quality ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%), significantly higher than preference to the first iteration of prompt based LLM-generated response (<15% for both tone or overall quality) with P -value less than .001.

links.outcome: Hallucinated clinical information in AI-drafted patient messages
links.effect: Hallucinations occurred in 7 (6%) of 116 original responses; none were found in responses from the 200-message validation set using the optimized prompt.
links.quote: Interesting, 7 (6%) of the 116 original messages from the test set were found to contain hallucinated information in the LLM responses.

links.outcome: Patient preference for human versus initial-prompt AI response tone and quality
links.effect: Patients preferred human-generated responses for tone (N = 159, 68%) and overall quality (N = 160, 69%) over initial-prompt AI responses.
links.quote: There was notable preference for human-generated responses in the first phase of evaluation for both tone ( N = 159, 68%) and quality ( N = 160, 69%) ( Figure 4A ).

links.outcome: Patient advisors’ ability to identify AI-generated responses when blinded to authorship
links.effect: Patient advisors correctly identified AI-generated responses only 24% of the time; 50% were attributed to humans, and authorship was undetermined for 26%.
links.quote: As shown in Figure 5 , in the final round of patient evaluation, patients determined that 77% ( N = 192) of responses completely addressed patient questions, and patients correctly identified messages were AI-generated only 24% of the time.

links.effect: Patient preference for tone and quality increased from <15% to 62% with local prompt tuning.
links.quote: When comparing responses created from the final prompt to the initial prompt, patient preference shifted to the optimized prompt (V3) based LLM-generated responses for tone ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%) and quality ( Figure 4B , N = 154, 62%), significantly higher than preference to the first iteration of prompt based LLM-generated response (<15% for both tone or overall quality) with P -value less than .001.

links.effect: 45% of validation drafts required editing and 16% were rejected by physicians.
links.quote: Of the validation set of 200 newly selected messages reviewed by pilot physicians, 34% were ranked as “Send,” 45% as “Edit,” and 16% as “Reject,” the proportion of “Send” and “Edit” combined was much higher than the rank based on the first prompt ( Figure 3 , P -value <.01).

links.effect: 52% of patient feedback was negative for initial AI responses compared to 14% for human responses.
links.quote: Sentiment analysis revealed that 50% ( N = 117) positive toward human-generated messages, compared to 15% positive for original prompt based LLM-generated messages ( P -value <.01) ( Supplementary Figure S4 ), and 52% negative feedback toward responses generated based on the original prompt, compared to 14% negative for the human response.

links.effect: 6% of original messages contained hallucinated information in the LLM responses.
links.quote: Interesting, 7 (6%) of the 116 original messages from the test set were found to contain hallucinated information in the LLM responses.
